operations.name: Concrete Activity Enumeration Search
operations.description: Use when a question asks what activities, hobbies, or kinds/types of activities a person pursues, including 'besides' variants.
content: When a question asks what activities or hobbies a person pursues (including 'besides', 'apart from', or 'other than' an excluded topic), do not rely only on structured queries with predicate='activity' or abstract category phrases; activity facts are often embedded in event/preference/state memories with other predicates or in free-text descriptions.

Generate a list of concrete activity types common to the domain and run at least one hybrid or semantic/free-text search per type using participation phrasing (e.g., '[subject] presented at', '[subject] attends', '[subject] interned at') and without requiring the words 'activity' or 'hobby' to appear.

Before answering, if the retrieved set is missing concrete activities, widen memory_kinds beyond 'event' to include 'preference', 'profile', and 'state', and re-search each concrete activity name that appears anywhere in the session or evidence; verify the answer covers every enumerated activity type that has supporting evidence.
operations.reason: Creating merged Skill for concrete activity enumeration across domains.

operations.name: Concrete Value Term Search for Abstract Questions
operations.description: Use when a question asks for a concrete attribute value or describes an activity with abstract/functional wording and initial retrieval returns only generic memories.
content: When a question asks for the value of an attribute (breed, type, make, model, genre, cuisine) or describes an activity with abstract/evaluative wording (e.g., 'fun indoor area', 'rewarding experience'), do not stop after a single search that repeats only the category noun or abstract phrase; the supporting memory may express the value or activity directly with concrete terms.

Run at least one additional hybrid or keyword search using concrete value terms and synonyms (e.g., for dog breeds: 'Lab', 'Chihuahua', 'mix'; for indoor area: bed, toys, pads, crate, playpen) and inspect low-scoring results that contain these values.

Before answering from a generic memory or saying no information, check for a more specific memory about the same subject, inspect its versions if the current version lacks detail, and use the world_start of the most concrete matching memory as the answer basis when a time is asked.

operations.name: Expand recommendation queries beyond attribute terms
operations.description: When a question asks what item a person suggested or recommended, search with suggestion verbs and prefer explicit recommendation evidence.
content: If a question asks what a person suggested, recommended, or endorsed as fitting some description, do not build all searches around the descriptive terms; the supporting memory may state the recommendation without those terms.

Run an additional memory search using the person's name together with suggestion verbs such as 'recommends', 'suggested', 'suggests', 'advises', and if known the general category of the item, even if the attribute terms are absent.

Before answering, prefer a memory that explicitly records a recommendation or suggestion over one that merely matches the descriptive attributes; if none of the retrieved memories explicitly state a suggestion, keep searching before answering.

operations.name: Search emotion/appreciation statements for view questions
operations.description: When a question asks how a person views or regards something, search concrete emotion/appreciation terms before answering.
content: When a question asks how someone views or regards something, do not rely only on queries containing abstract words like view, perception, or opinion; those words may be absent from stored memories.

Run supplementary searches combining the person with concrete emotion/appreciation/relationship terms (e.g., grateful, thankful, loves, 'part of the family') and with the target entity, and inspect event and preference memories for explicit attitudinal statements.

Before answering, require evidence that states the person's view or feeling explicitly; if retrieved evidence only shows related behaviors or plans, continue searching instead of inferring the view from behavior alone.

operations.name: Health injury synonym and family-member retrieval
operations.description: When a question asks who was injured or affected by a health condition, use synonym expansions and per-family-member searches.
content: If a question asks about injuries, accidents, or health problems affecting a person or their family, do not answer from a single search using only the literal wording; memories may describe the event with related terms such as accident, injury, hurt, surgery, hospital, or specific body parts.

Run at least one supplementary search combining the person's name with synonyms of the health condition, and include queries for each named family member or relation when the question asks 'who' in a group.

Before answering, check that the retrieved evidence covers every person the question asks about; if only the main subject is found, continue searching with family-relation terms until relevant memories for all individuals are retrieved or exhausted.

operations.name: Retrieve explicit ailment names for cause-linked health questions
operations.description: When a question asks what ailment a person has due to a cause, broaden retrieval to health-related memories and specific condition terms.
content: When a question asks which ailment or medical condition a person faces due to a stated cause, run at least one supplementary search for the person's health-related memories using terms like '<person> health', '<person> doctor', '<person> diagnosis', 'medical condition', or 'ER visit' without repeating the cause qualifier.
Treat event memories that name a specific condition as stronger evidence than generic state memories about health struggles; answer with the named condition when present.
If initial searches return only generic health descriptions, issue further searches for plausible condition terms before concluding insufficient evidence.

operations.name: Broaden memory kinds for stress-relief queries
operations.description: When a question asks what relieves stress, search across all memory kinds including state and plan.
content: If a question asks about a person's stress relievers, relaxation methods, or ways to unwind, do not restrict memory_kinds to 'preference' and 'event'; include 'state' and 'plan' memories because stress-relief evidence can be stored as emotional states or planned calming activities.

Run supplementary searches with stress/relaxation vocabulary (de-stress, relax, calm, unwind, cope, guilty) across all memory_kinds, and accept indirect evidence such as a person feeling guilty about a comfort behavior or planning an outing to de-stress.

Before answering, verify that state and plan memories were searched; if the initial retrieval lacks them, issue a broader memory_kind search and treat relevant state/plan memories as supporting evidence.

operations.name: Expand health-incident queries with diagnostic terms
operations.description: When a question asks what health scares or incidents someone experienced, retrieve memories with specific diagnoses or symptoms.
content: When the question asks about health scares, health incidents, medical problems, or illnesses experienced by one or more named people, do not rely only on generic 'health scare' or 'health issue' vocabulary. Run additional keyword or structured searches using concrete medical condition and symptom terms (diagnoses, body-part pains, ER or hospital events) and predicate values such as 'health_issue'.
For multi-person questions, run separate searches for each named person in addition to the combined query, because a single combined query can fail to surface each person's specific incident.
Before answering, verify that every named person in the question has retrieved evidence; if a person is missing, issue additional varied searches before finalizing the answer.

operations.name: Search emotional outcome memories for activity-effect questions
operations.description: When a question asks what an activity makes a person feel, search for memories explicitly linking the activity to an emotion.
content: If a user asks what a person's activity makes them or how an activity affects their feelings, do not stop after retrieving general activity, career, or performance memories that lack an emotional outcome; the answer may be in enrichment memories that state the person's feelings toward the activity.

Before answering, run a supplementary memory search combining the person's name, the activity, and emotion terms (e.g., 'happy', 'joy', 'fulfillment', 'enjoy'), and a search for emotional-state memories (e.g., '<person> feels', '<person> happiness').

Judge evidence sufficiency against the asked effect: if no retrieved memory states that the activity makes the person feel that emotion, do not substitute unrelated traits such as determination or success; keep searching for a direct activity-emotion link.

operations.name: Verify per-person evidence for multi-subject attribution questions
operations.description: When a question asks why multiple people feel a certain way, verify evidence covers each named person before answering.
content: Before answering a question that names two or more people as subjects (e.g., 'Why do X and Y admire Z?'), check that the retrieved evidence explicitly covers every named person; if only one is covered, do not answer for the group.

Run an additional hybrid or keyword search for each missing person individually, using '<person> <topic> admires/inspired/likes/enjoys', because the relevant detail may be embedded in a broader preference or event memory.

Answer only with reasons that are explicitly supported for each named person; if a person's reason remains unsupported after expanded searches, state that unsupported portion explicitly instead of borrowing evidence from another person.

operations.name: Search routine activities for grief coping sources
operations.description: When a question asks what helped someone cope during grief, search current routines and activities, not only memories mentioning the loss.
content: If a question asks what helped someone find peace, comfort, or cope after a loss or difficult time, do not limit retrieval to memories mentioning the grief; run additional hybrid/keyword searches for the person's current routines, activities, hobbies, and places (e.g., yoga, walking, nature, gardening).

Treat recent event and preference memories as evidence even when they do not mention the loss, as long as they explicitly describe peace, calm, clarity, or comfort; prefer the most recent version of each memory.
If the first search returns only memories of the loss itself, broaden the query with activity and interest nouns from the person's profile instead of repeating the same grief-focused query.
